client: I've been really anxious about this networking event coming up next week — just thinking about it makes my heart race and I feel kind of sick to my stomach. I have to walk into a room full of strangers in my field and introduce myself, and I honestly don't know how I'm going to get through it. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give it a shot.
therapist: It means a lot that you gave this a shot, and those physical sensations — the racing heart, the nausea — are your body's very real response to something that feels genuinely threatening, so there's nothing "wrong" with you for feeling this way. What I'm curious about is what your mind is telling you in those moments when you imagine walking into that room — like, what's the worst thing you picture happening?

client: Honestly, the worst thing I picture is walking up to someone, opening my mouth, and just... going completely blank. Like, I'll have nothing interesting to say, they'll give me that polite smile and then look for an excuse to talk to literally anyone else, and I'll be standing there alone feeling like an idiot. And the worst part is I keep telling myself that's probably exactly what's going to happen, because it's kind of happened before.
therapist: That image you're describing — the blank mind, the polite brush-off — sounds really painful, and it makes complete sense that a past experience like that would make your brain treat it as a certainty this time. But I want to gently pause on that word "probably," because there's a difference between something that *has* happened once and something that *will* happen — and our anxious minds are really skilled at collapsing that gap. Can you tell me a little more about that past experience — did *everyone* walk away, or were there also moments that went differently than your brain is currently giving them credit for?

client: Okay, I mean... no, not everyone walked away. There was actually one person I ended up talking to for like twenty minutes about a project we were both working on, and it felt pretty natural. But my brain keeps kind of glossing over that part and zeroing in on the two or three awkward moments, and I'm not sure just pointing that out is going to make me feel less terrified next week.
therapist: That twenty-minute conversation is actually really important evidence — your brain has been quietly hiding it from you while putting the awkward moments on a loop, which is such a classic trick anxiety plays. You're right that just *noticing* this pattern doesn't flip a switch and make the fear disappear, but what it does is give you something real to hold onto when the dread starts to spiral. I'm wondering — what do you think made that twenty-minute conversation flow so naturally, and could we use that as a kind of blueprint for next week?

client: I think it worked because we had something concrete in common to talk about — like, the topic was already there, so I didn't have to come up with something clever or impressive out of thin air. But I guess my worry is that a "blueprint" sounds nice in theory, except what if I walk in next week and I can't find anyone who has that obvious common ground, and then I'm back to square one with nothing to say. It feels like that conversation was kind of a lucky accident more than something I could actually replicate on purpose.
therapist: What you just identified — that having a concrete shared topic took the pressure off performing or being impressive — is actually a really powerful insight, and it's not luck, it's a *condition* you can deliberately create. At a networking event in your own field, common ground isn't rare; it's essentially the whole room, and you could even go in with one or two genuine questions about what people are working on, so the topic is already there waiting. What might it feel like to walk in with the goal of being *curious* rather than impressive — does that shift anything for you, even slightly?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way — curious instead of impressive — something does shift a little, like the pressure feels slightly less suffocating for a second. But then I immediately think, what if I ask someone a question and they give a short answer and the conversation just dies right there, and I'm standing there having to scramble again. I think my fear isn't just about having nothing to say, it's also about being seen as someone who doesn't belong in that room in the first place.
therapist: That fear of not belonging — of being *seen through* as someone who shouldn't be there — feels like it runs a lot deeper than just awkward small talk, and I really appreciate you naming it because it sounds like the heart of what's actually driving the anxiety. It's worth noticing that everyone in that room has likely felt some version of that too, even the people who look completely at ease, because that feeling of not belonging is remarkably common among people who are actually quite capable. I'm curious — when you imagine someone *else* stumbling through a conversation at that event, would you see them as someone who doesn't belong, or would you feel something different toward them?

client: No, I'd probably feel bad for them and want to help them out somehow, not judge them as someone who doesn't belong. And I can see what you're doing there — like, I'm applying this totally different standard to myself than I would to anyone else. But knowing that intellectually and actually *feeling* it in the moment when my heart is pounding and everyone seems so confident around me... those feel like really different things, and I'm not sure how to close that gap.
therapist: You've just named one of the most honest and important things a person can recognize — that insight and felt experience live in different parts of us, and intellectual understanding alone doesn't automatically rewire the emotional response in the heat of the moment. That gap is real, and the way we start to close it isn't just through thinking differently but through small, lived experiences that slowly give your nervous system new evidence to work with. So I'm wondering — what might it look like to set yourself one tiny, low-stakes intention for next week, not "have a great event," but something small enough that even an anxious version of you could actually do it?

client: Maybe something like... just asking one person one genuine question, and that's it, that's the whole goal. Like, if I do that one thing, I can consider it a success regardless of how the rest of the night goes. But I'm already a little worried that in the moment I'll talk myself out of even that, because anxiety has this way of making even tiny things feel impossible when I'm actually standing there.
therapist: That one-question goal is genuinely perfect — it's small enough to be achievable and meaningful enough to actually count as evidence against the story that you don't belong there. And your worry about talking yourself out of it in the moment is worth taking seriously, so it might help to think of it like a commitment you make *now*, before anxiety gets a vote — almost like you're making a deal with tonight-you on behalf of next-week-you. What do you think would help you remember that commitment when you're standing at the door and your heart is racing — is there something you could say to yourself, or even do beforehand, that might act as an anchor?

client: I think maybe I could remind myself of that twenty-minute conversation — like, literally just bring that specific memory to mind before I walk in, as proof that it's actually happened for me before. But I'll be honest, there's a part of me that feels a little silly thinking about doing that, like I'm giving myself a pep talk in a parking lot before going into a work event. I guess I'm just not sure if something that simple could actually hold up against how loud the anxiety gets in that moment.
therapist: There's nothing silly about it — what you're actually doing is deliberately giving your brain accurate information to counter the distorted story anxiety is trying to sell you, and that's not a pep talk, that's a genuinely effective strategy. The anxiety will probably still be loud, but loud doesn't mean *right*, and having one concrete memory to point to is a lot harder for your brain to argue with than a general "I'll be fine." I'm curious — as you imagine yourself in that parking lot, bringing that conversation to mind, what do you notice happening in your body right now, even just slightly?

client: Honestly, when I actually picture that moment and bring that conversation to mind, there's something that loosens just a tiny bit in my chest — like it's not completely gone, but it's not quite as tight. I'm kind of surprised by that, because I expected it to feel like nothing. I'm still not fully convinced it'll hold up in the actual moment next week, but I guess it's at least something real to try.
therapist: That loosening in your chest — even just a tiny bit — is actually your nervous system responding to real evidence, and that's not nothing, that's exactly how this kind of change works, in small increments rather than one dramatic shift. You don't need to be fully convinced it'll work; you just need to be willing to try it, and it sounds like you're already there. As you head toward next week, I want to ask — how are you feeling about yourself right now, in this conversation, compared to when you first sat down and weren't even sure talking would help?

client: I think I feel... a little less alone with it, which I wasn't expecting. Like, I came in here kind of braced to be told to just think positive or push through it, and instead it feels like we actually looked at something real together. I'm still nervous about next week, but it doesn't feel quite as inevitable that it's going to be a disaster.
therapist: What you just described — feeling less alone with it, and the disaster feeling less inevitable — that's genuinely meaningful progress, and you did that by being willing to look honestly at your own experience rather than just pushing the fear away. The nervousness still being there is completely okay; it means you care, and you've now got something real to bring with you — one concrete memory, one small goal, and a little more accurate picture of what you're actually capable of. As you go into next week, I hope you'll be as gentle with yourself as you would be with that stranger you imagined stumbling through a conversation — you deserve at least that much.
